title: The cards of power
subtitle: In which the visit is tallied, Hormuz is refused, two ministers shake hands after four years, and Paris fills a square that once belonged to the Revolution.

body:
Yesterday a plan still lay on the table. Today the refusal lies beside it. Between those two papers, in New York, two men shake hands who have not sat together in four years. In Paris a square fills that once belonged to the Revolution.

I. Eight points, one refusal

Beijing keeps the books on the visit in eight lines: tariff cuts of thirty billion dollars on goods that do not frighten either capital, a council for trade, a channel for accidents involving artificial intelligence. November is named for the next round; Shenzhen for APEC, Miami for the G20. The files that cut — Taiwan, the rare earths, the deeper locks on machines — stay blunt. The two thrones have drawn nearer without swapping blades. 1 2

In the Gulf the answer Saturday left hanging arrives. Trump rejects the seven-day plan on the White House lawn. He will talk, he says; he will not talk on these terms. Araghchi waits for the mediators to speak with an official mouth. The tankers keep a longer watch than the diplomats. 5 6

II. Twenty minutes

In the hall of nations Johann Wadephul and Sergey Lavrov take one table. Barely twenty minutes. Wadephul warns against the road already taken against Germany, Europe and NATO, and asks that grain be allowed across the Black Sea. Afterwards Lavrov says he heard nothing he did not already know; the statement could have been read to him by telephone. A handshake. The lights in the hall stay on. So does the cold. 3

China's vice-president, Han Zheng, standing in the same building, asks that the order built after the last world war be kept. On the ground the handshake changes no line. Trump tells Zelenskyy, in public, to come to terms with Putin. 4 7

III. The square that fills

In Paris the estimates run from seven to eight hundred thousand along the Concorde. Leo XIV speaks of a thirst for peace, and of machines that must serve a human life rather than sit in judgment over it. A country that keeps church and state in separate rooms finds its square full. Then the road turns toward Lourdes. 8

IV. At the edge of the page

While the cards lie in New York and Paris, Saturday writes elsewhere. In Dera Ismail Khan a bomber kills twelve at a police post and wounds thirty. Bangkok names the flood a disaster: at least two dead, tens of thousands driven from their rooms. A nor'easter on the American seaboard cancels four hundred flights, takes the light from sixty-eight thousand houses and a life in New York. Off Kamchatka the fishing vessel Triumf burns. In Gauteng gunmen walk into taverns; seventeen die in Carletonville, and other counts speak of two massacres and more than twenty. Gaza's health ministry puts the dead of this war above seventy-four thousand. 9 10

The chronicler's close

Three cards lie open in the great rooms. At the edge of the page lie those who make no speech. Whether Tehran deals again, whether Lourdes finds other words than the Concorde — that belongs to the next leaf.
